---
title: "Advanced: save standalone outputs from R"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Optional"}
This page is for users who are comfortable with R and want to save **standalone output files** directly from R into their DNAnexus project.

You do **not** need this workflow to complete this core tutorial. For most analyses, your `[DX]` notebook is the main record of your work.
:::

## Why would you need this?

Earlier in the tutorial, we saw that saving your `[DX]` notebook preserves the notebook and the outputs displayed inside it.

Sometimes you may also want a separate file in your DNAnexus project.

Examples include:

- an approved summary table in CSV format;
- a figure saved as a PNG or PDF;
- a model result saved as a separate file; or
- another analysis output that you want to use in a later workflow.

A file created by R in the temporary JupyterLab environment is **not automatically saved to the DNAnexus project**.

This page shows a simple way for experienced R users to upload an approved standalone file directly from R.

## 1. The basic workflow

The overall process is:

```text
R creates a file
      ↓
Temporary JupyterLab environment
      ↓
R helper uploads the file to DNAnexus project
      ↓
Persistent DNAnexus project
```

The upload uses the DNAnexus command-line tool behind the scenes.

You do **not** need to open a terminal or use the command line yourself.

## 2. Set your workspace

Before using the upload helper, tell R where **your own workspace** is in the DNAnexus project.

Start with:

```r
my_workspace <- "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_WORKSPACE"
```

Replace `REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_WORKSPACE` with the path to your own workspace **before you try to upload anything**.

For example, a workshop workspace might have a path such as:

```text
/participant-XX/
```

and a research-project workspace might be inside:

```text
/Users/<your-name>/
```

Use the actual path to **your own** workspace.

::: {.callout-warning title="Set your own workspace before continuing"}
Do not copy another participant's or researcher's workspace path.

The helper function below is designed to stop with an error if you leave:

```text
REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_WORKSPACE
```

unchanged.
:::

You can check what you have entered by running:

```r
my_workspace
```

Make sure the displayed path is the workspace where you intend to save your files.

## 3. Define the helper function

Add the following function to your R notebook:

```r
save_to_dnanexus <- function(
  file,
  destination = my_workspace
) {

  if (!file.exists(file)) {
    stop("File not found: ", file)
  }

  if (
    !exists("my_workspace", inherits = TRUE) ||
    identical(destination, "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_WORKSPACE") ||
    !is.character(destination) ||
    length(destination) != 1 ||
    !nzchar(destination)
  ) {
    stop(
      "Your DNAnexus workspace has not been set. ",
      "Set 'my_workspace' to your own workspace before uploading."
    )
  }

  result <- system2(
    "dx",
    c(
      "upload",
      file,
      "--destination", destination,
      "--brief"
    ),
    stdout = TRUE,
    stderr = TRUE
  )

  status <- attr(result, "status")

  if (!is.null(status) && status != 0) {
    stop(
      "Upload failed:\n",
      paste(result, collapse = "\n")
    )
  }

  cat(
    "File successfully saved to DNAnexus:\n",
    destination, basename(file), "\n"
  )

  invisible(result)
}
```

This function:

1. checks that the file exists;
2. checks that you have set a workspace rather than leaving the placeholder unchanged;
3. uploads the file to your workspace in the DNAnexus project; and
4. reports whether the upload succeeded.

## 4. Save an output file

For example, suppose you have created an approved summary table:

```r
results <- aggregate(
  age ~ sex,
  data = dat,
  FUN = mean
)
```

Save it as a CSV file in the temporary JupyterLab environment:

```r
write.csv(
  results,
  "age_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Then upload it to the workspace you defined earlier:

```r
save_to_dnanexus("age_summary.csv")
```

You do not need to type the destination again. The function uses `my_workspace`.

::: {.callout-note title="The destination is persistent"}
The file is first created in the temporary JupyterLab environment.

The `save_to_dnanexus()` function then uploads a copy into your workspace in the DNAnexus project.

Once uploaded, the project copy is persistent.
:::

## 5. Save a figure

The same approach works for figures.

For example:

```r
png("age_blood_pressure.png", width = 1200, height = 900)

plot(
  dat$age,
  dat$systolic_bp,
  xlab = "Age (years)",
  ylab = "Systolic blood pressure",
  main = "Synthetic training data"
)

dev.off()
```

Then upload the figure:

```r
save_to_dnanexus("age_blood_pressure.png")
```

The same `my_workspace` destination is used automatically.

## 6. Check the DNAnexus project

After the upload, refresh the **DNAnexus project browser**.

The new file should appear in your workspace.

You can then use it like any other persistent project file.

::: {.callout-tip title="Save only files you actually need"}
Do not upload every intermediate file generated during an analysis.

Keep your workspace tidy and save only outputs that are useful for your analysis or that you need to use later.
:::

## 7. Data safety still applies

This helper makes it easy to move files from the temporary JupyterLab environment into persistent DNAnexus project storage.

It does **not** change whether a file is safe to export from DNAnexus.

For real MCPS research projects, this is an important distinction:

```text
Temporary JupyterLab
        ↓
Persistent DNAnexus project
```

is part of normal project work.

By contrast:

```text
DNAnexus
        ↓
Local computer
```

is subject to the MCPS data-access rules described earlier in this tutorial.

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not use this to export research data"}
This function saves files **within the DNAnexus project**.

It does not give permission to download individual-level MCPS research data to your local computer.

Individual-level MCPS research data must remain within the approved DNAnexus environment.
:::

## 8. When should you use this?

For most analyses, you can simply keep your work in your `[DX]` notebook.

Use this approach when you specifically need a **standalone persistent file** in the DNAnexus project.

A useful rule is:

| Need | Recommended approach |
|---|---|
| Keep code and analysis together | Save the `[DX]` notebook |
| Display a table or figure | Keep it in the notebook |
| Save a standalone CSV/PNG/PDF for later use | Upload it to the project |
| Move individual-level MCPS data to your computer | **Do not do this** |

## 9. A final note for workshop participants

The standard MCPS workshops do not require this technique.

The instructors will provide the workshop notebooks and shared data in advance, and most workshop outputs can simply remain in your `[DX]` notebook.

This page is included so that more experienced R users know that it is possible to persist standalone outputs directly from R without using a terminal.

::: {.callout-success title="Advanced workflow complete"}
You now have an optional R function for saving approved standalone outputs directly into your DNAnexus project.

For day-to-day work, remember the simpler workflow:

**Work in your `[DX]` notebook → save regularly → end your JupyterLab session.**
:::
